opus-5.5.text:
I think the most exciting thing about AlphaEvolve is that it's a general-purpose tool. It isn't built for one problem. Any time you can write down what a good solution looks like, so you have a way to automatically evaluate a candidate, AlphaEvolve can search the space of programs and keep improving on what's there. That covers an enormous range of problems.

We've already seen real impact inside Google. It found a heuristic for scheduling jobs across our data centers that recovers a meaningful fraction of compute that was otherwise being stranded. It sped up a key matrix multiplication kernel used in training Gemini, which means AlphaEvolve is helping make the models that power it more efficient. It even proposed changes to hardware circuit designs. These aren't toy demos. They're deployed and running at scale, and small percentage gains at Google's scale translate into very large savings.

On the scientific side, we pointed it at a set of open problems in mathematics, things like combinatorial constructions and packing problems. In a good share of them it matched the best known results, and in some it found better ones. It also improved on Strassen's decades-old result for multiplying four-by-four complex matrices. So it can contribute genuinely new knowledge, not just optimize existing systems.

Looking ahead, I see the greatest potential in two places. The first is algorithm discovery and engineering optimization broadly: logistics, chip design, compilers, energy systems, anywhere efficiency matters and you can measure it. The second, which excites me most personally, is science. Many fields have problems where verifying a solution is easy but finding one is incredibly hard: materials, drug discovery, parts of physics and mathematics. A system like AlphaEvolve can become a real collaborator for scientists there. It proposes ideas, the evaluator checks them, and humans bring the intuition about which problems matter and how to frame them.

That collaboration is really the key. The best results we've seen come from experts working with the system, framing the problem and the evaluation function well, and then letting it explore far more of the space than any person could. If we can put that capability into the hands of researchers and engineers everywhere, I think the impact could be very broad.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaEvolve is suited to problems where a candidate can be automatically evaluated against what a good solution looks like.

r002.rationale: It says experts let AlphaEvolve explore far more of the solution space than any person could.

r003.rationale: The response describes broad exploration and new discoveries, but does not state that AlphaEvolve finds counterintuitive strategies humans might not imagine.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about AlphaEvolve is that it's really a general-purpose engine for discovering better algorithms, and so the question of where it has the greatest impact comes down to where algorithms are the bottleneck. And it turns out that's almost everywhere.

The place where we've already seen very concrete impact is inside our own infrastructure. AlphaEvolve found a scheduling heuristic for Borg, which is the system that orchestrates compute across Google's data centers, and that recovered on the order of 0.7 percent of our worldwide compute. That sounds small, but at Google scale that's a very large amount of resources that are now available for other work. It also improved parts of the Gemini training stack, so there's this nice recursive flavor where the system is helping make the models that power it more efficient. And it contributed to the design of our TPUs by simplifying some of the arithmetic circuits. So in the near term, I'd say the biggest impact is in these critical pieces of infrastructure that the world increasingly runs on, where even a one percent improvement compounds enormously.

The second area, and the one I'm personally most excited about, is scientific and mathematical discovery. AlphaEvolve found a way to multiply four-by-four complex matrices with 48 multiplications, improving on Strassen's result from 1969. That's a problem people have been staring at for over fifty years. And across a set of about fifty open problems in mathematics, it matched the best known results in most cases and improved on them in about twenty percent. What that tells you is that this isn't just an optimization tool, it's a tool that can push the frontier of human knowledge in areas where very smart people have already looked hard.

And then longer term, I think the real potential is in domains like materials science, drug discovery, sustainability, anywhere you can frame a problem as "here's a candidate solution and here's a way to score it automatically." That verifiability is the key ingredient. Once you have a reliable evaluator, AlphaEvolve can explore a space of solutions far more broadly and persistently than any human team could. So the honest answer is that the greatest impact will probably come from problems we haven't even thought to pose to it yet, in fields where experts realize they can write down a scoring function for something they care about.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaEvolve is suited to problems with a reliable evaluator that can score candidate solutions automatically.

r002.rationale: It says AlphaEvolve can explore solution spaces more broadly and persistently than any human team could.

r003.rationale: The response describes broad exploration and problems people have not yet posed, but does not clearly state that AlphaEvolve can find counterintuitive strategies humans might not imagine.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is in problems where you can automatically check whether a proposed solution is better. In those settings, AlphaEvolve can explore ideas, test them, and use that feedback to keep improving.

Computing infrastructure is a particularly exciting example. If you can improve an algorithm that runs millions or billions of times, or make better use of the hardware in a data center, even a small efficiency gain can have a substantial impact. You’re saving resources, reducing energy use, and potentially making more computation available for science.

But what excites me most is the possibility of helping researchers discover things they wouldn’t have thought to try. The researcher still has a crucial role in choosing the problem and defining what success means. AlphaEvolve can then expand the space of solutions we’re able to explore. So I see the near-term impact in optimization, and the longer-term potential in scientific and mathematical discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaEvolve is suited to problems where a proposed solution can be automatically checked for improvement.

r002.rationale: It says AlphaEvolve can expand the space of solutions explored, but does not clearly state that it can keep exploring beyond a human programmer’s practical limits.

r003.rationale: The response says AlphaEvolve could help researchers discover things they would not have thought to try.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the greatest potential is in improving the computational infrastructure that we all depend on. If you can discover a better algorithm for a task that runs millions or billions of times, even a small improvement can have a substantial impact on cost, energy use, and what becomes possible. That could mean making data centers more efficient, improving chip design, or speeding up the computations used to train AI systems.

The key is that we need a reliable way to evaluate a proposed solution. When we can measure whether something is correct and whether it performs better, we can use that feedback to search for improvements that people might not have thought of. I’m particularly excited about applying that approach to scientific problems where computation is a bottleneck. Better algorithms can give researchers the ability to explore questions that were previously too expensive to tackle.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaEvolve is suited to tasks where correctness and performance can be reliably measured, enabling search for improvements.

r002.rationale: It describes searching for improvements but does not say AlphaEvolve can continue exploring beyond a human programmer’s practical limits.

r003.rationale: It says the search can find improvements people might not have thought of, conveying counterintuitive strategies humans might not imagine.
